newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon says Japan identifies Red Army guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon says Japan identifies Red Army guerrillas.

text.p: Lebanese Prosecutor General Adnan Addoum said on Tuesday Japan had provided documents identifying five people arrested in Beirut as members of the Japanese Red Army guerrillas.

Although Addoum said he would need another 24 hours to confirm their identities, a senior judicial source said he was certain they were the long-sought guerrillas. Another three Japanese citizens and one Lebanese woman were also under arrest.
The source named the five alleged guerrillas as Kazua Tohira, 44, Hisashi Matsuda, 48, Mariko Yamamoto, 56, Masao Adachi, 57 and 49-year-old Kozo Okamoto.

Okamoto took part in the May 1972 massacre at Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 24 people died and 100 were injured. He was captured and sentenced to life in prison but was released in a Palestinian-Israeli prisoner swap in May 1985.
Addoum told reporters a Japanese security delegation gave him documents identifying five of the eight Japanese citizens arrested in Beirut as Red Army guerrillas.

"We will open investigations to confirm their identity within 24 hours and if it proves that they have committed crimes in Lebanon, they will be tried here," Addoum said, explaining they could face forgery charges.

The case has been mired in confusion since February 18 when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in Tokyo that Lebanese officials had told him of the arrest of six Japanese Red Army suspects.
Lebanon's foreign ministry initially confirmed the reports but last week Lebanese security sources denied holding any Japanese citizens.

"The whole issue had started with information about a group of Asians forging passports. We started pursuing them and detained them. We still have to further investigate before we can charge them," Addoum said.

"After initial investigations we will decide whether to charge the detainees or not. We will find out whether they had committed any crimes in Lebanon or not. If yes, they will be tried in Lebanon," Addoum said.

Judicial sources said anyone convicted of forgery could face up to three years in prison before Lebanon begins negotiating their handover to Japan. Lebanon and Japan do not have an extradition treaty.

On Monday a Japanese envoy indicated Tokyo no longer expected Lebanon to extradict them immediately but hoped to get them after Lebanese justice runs its course. Tokyo officials had said they were ready to send an aircraft to Beirut now to bring them home.

The Red Army, founded in 1971, is allied to hardline anti-Israeli Palestinian factions. The Bekaa Valley was a haven during Lebanon's 1975-90 civil war for a wide range of guerrilla groups, including Lebanese Islamists and Marxists, Palestinian factions, Kurds and the Red Army.
